body:
Gujarat in ancient and early-medieval India

Gujarat occupied an important position in western India because it connected the Arabian Sea coast with the inland regions of Malwa, Rajasthan and the Deccan. Agricultural settlements supported political authority, while towns and ports connected the region with long-distance trade routes.

Between the early centuries of the Common Era and the 8th century CE, 2 important ruling groups shaped Gujarat's political history: the Western Kshatrapas and the Maitrakas of Vallabhi. They belonged to different periods and political traditions.

  • Western Kshatrapas: Rulers of Shaka origin who controlled substantial parts of Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa from approximately the 1st to the late 4th century CE.
  • Gupta expansion: Chandragupta II defeated the last Western Kshatrapas around the end of the 4th century CE, bringing important western territories under Gupta control.
  • Maitrakas: A regional dynasty that emerged in Saurashtra in the late 5th century CE and ruled from Vallabhi into the later 8th century CE.

The Maitrakas did not directly succeed Rudradaman or his dynasty. The Western Kshatrapas ended around the close of the 4th century CE; the Maitrakas emerged in the political conditions that followed the weakening of Gupta authority.

Important geographical names

Saurashtra and Girnar

Saurashtra refers to the Kathiawar peninsula of Gujarat. Junagadh, near Mount Girnar, is particularly important because the rock inscriptions there preserve information about the Mauryas, the Western Kshatrapas and the Guptas. The historical name Girinagara is associated with this area.

Anarta, Malwa and Lata

Anarta was an ancient regional name associated with parts of Gujarat, particularly its northern and northwestern areas. Malwa, including Ujjain, lay farther inland and connected western India with important overland routes. Lata generally denoted southern Gujarat and the region associated with Bharuch. These historical names should not be treated as having boundaries identical to modern districts.

Vallabhi and Bharuch

Vallabhi, near present-day Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district, became the Maitraka capital. Bharukachchha, the ancient name of Bharuch, was a major trading outlet on the western coast. The 2 places had different political and commercial roles and should not be confused.

Understanding the dynastic names

The term Kshatrapa, related to the Persian tradition of satraps, originally indicated a governor or territorial ruler. In western India it became a royal title. Mahakshatrapa meant Great Kshatrapa and generally denoted a more senior ruling position.

The name Maitraka refers to a ruling family rather than an administrative title. Its rulers developed a regional kingdom centred on Vallabhi. Their history illustrates how military leaders and regional chiefs could acquire royal authority as larger empires weakened.

Prelims focus

  • Western Kshatrapas: Shaka rulers associated with western India, especially Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa.
  • Maitrakas: Rulers of Vallabhi in Saurashtra, from approximately the late 5th to later 8th century CE.
  • Junagadh and Girnar: Associated with the Sudarshana Lake inscriptions.
  • Vallabhi: Near present-day Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district.
  • Bharukachchha: Ancient Bharuch, an important western trading outlet.
  • Trap: The Western Kshatrapas and Maitrakas were not branches of the same dynasty.

[NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 35–38; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts-I, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed p. 114; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Numismatics, Western Kshatrapa Coinage: An Introduction, section 1; Annette Schmiedchen, Maitrakas, The Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, dynastic history, first published 2021; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat's Political Setting: From the Western Kshatrapas to the Maitrakas

body:
Who were the Western Kshatrapas?

The Western Kshatrapas, also called Western Satraps, were rulers of Shaka origin who established political authority in parts of western India. Their territory changed over time, but Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa were especially important regions.

The Western Kshatrapas were not a single ruler or a single uninterrupted family line. Their history is generally organised around 2 principal ruling families: the Kshaharatas and the Kardamakas.

The 2 principal ruling families

FamilyImportant rulerCore association
KshaharataBhumakaEarly ruler known through coins.
KshaharataNahapanaExpansion in western India and conflict with the Satavahanas.
KardamakaChastanaLeading early ruler of the Kardamaka line.
KardamakaRudradaman IMajor ruler associated with the Junagadh inscription and Sudarshana Lake restoration.

Nahapana and the Satavahanas

Nahapana exercised power over parts of southern Gujarat and adjoining western regions. His political position brought the Kshaharatas into conflict with the Satavahanas, whose influence extended over parts of the Deccan.

An important fact is that the Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni overstruck many silver coins originally issued by Nahapana. An overstruck coin is an older coin impressed with new marks or symbols by another ruler. In this case, it demonstrates the struggle for control between the Kshaharatas and the Satavahanas.

Chastana and the Kardamakas

Chastana was the leading early ruler of the Kardamaka line, which became the more enduring branch of Western Kshatrapa rule. The family exercised authority in important parts of Gujarat, Saurashtra and western Malwa. Rudradaman I, Chastana's grandson, became one of its best-known rulers during the 2nd century CE.

The Kardamaka rulers retained the Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa titles. These titles could distinguish junior and senior ruling positions. Their exact political significance depended on the period and individual ruler; they should not be interpreted as permanently fixed modern administrative posts.

Rudradaman's political importance

Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription presents him as the ruler of an extensive western territory that included Anarta, Saurashtra and Kachchha, together with other regions. It also claims victories over neighbouring powers.

The inscription states that Rudradaman defeated a ruler called Satakarni on 2 occasions but spared him because of a close relationship. This is evidence of continued political rivalry between the Western Kshatrapas and the Satavahana world.

Keep the 2 Satavahana connections separate: Gautamiputra Satakarni is associated with the overstriking of Nahapana's coins. Rudradaman's inscription refers to victories over a Satakarni, whose precise identification is not certain. These facts should not be merged into a single event.

Coins and economic activity

Coinage is especially important for understanding Western Kshatrapa rule. Many rulers issued silver coins bearing a royal bust and inscriptions. The names and titles on coins help distinguish rulers, while the widespread circulation of silver coins indicates the importance of monetary exchange.

A characteristic silver coin of the Kardamaka period commonly has the ruler's head on the front. Its reverse bears a three-arched hill symbol, usually accompanied by a sun and crescent, with a ruler-name or title inscription in Brahmi script. Some earlier coins also carried Kharoshthi legends. Traces of Greek-style lettering appear on the front of many issues. Many later Western Kshatrapa coins are dated in the Shaka era.

Trade routes and ports

Western India benefited from both inland and maritime trade. Ujjain was an important inland centre in Malwa, while Bharukachchha or Bharuch connected inland regions with seaborne commerce. Other western coastal outlets also participated in trade.

Control over productive territory, towns and commercial routes helped rulers obtain resources. It would be incorrect, however, to assume that the entire western coast or every trading settlement remained under a single Western Kshatrapa ruler throughout the dynasty's history.

The end of Western Kshatrapa power

By the late 4th century CE, the Guptas expanded into western India. Chandragupta II defeated the last Western Kshatrapas, and important areas of Gujarat and Malwa passed under Gupta authority. The Western Kshatrapa political tradition therefore belongs mainly to the centuries before the rise of the Maitrakas.

Prelims focus

  • Kshaharata rulers: Bhumaka and Nahapana.
  • Kardamaka rulers: Chastana and Rudradaman I.
  • Gautamiputra Satakarni: Associated with overstriking Nahapana's coins.
  • Rudradaman I: A Mahakshatrapa and an important ruler of the 2nd century CE.
  • Western Kshatrapa silver coins: Royal bust, Brahmi legend and characteristic hill symbol.
  • Chandragupta II: Defeated the last Western Kshatrapas.
  • Trap: Nahapana and Rudradaman belonged to different ruling families.

[NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 35 and 38; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts-I, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed p. 114; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Numismatics, Western Kshatrapa Coinage: An Introduction, sections 1–4 and 6; F. Kielhorn, Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman, Epigraphia Indica, vol. 8, 1906, pp. 42–49; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Western Kshatrapas: Ruling Families, Important Kings and Trade

body:
Why the Junagadh inscription matters

The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is among the most important records of ancient Gujarat. It was engraved on a rock near Girnar at Junagadh and is associated with Shaka year 72, approximately 150 CE.

Its language is Classical Sanskrit and its script is Brahmi. It is an important early example of a royal prashasti, or inscription praising the accomplishments of a ruler, written in elaborate Sanskrit prose.

Prashasti

A prashasti is a composition praising a ruler or patron, often describing victories, virtues, ancestry and public works. It can preserve important historical facts, although its words of praise should not automatically be read as neutral descriptions.

The inscription is especially valuable because it connects Rudradaman's reign with the history of the Sudarshana Lake, an artificial reservoir near Girnar. The lake's history extends across several dynasties.

How the Sudarshana Lake developed

Construction under Chandragupta Maurya

The reservoir was originally constructed during the reign of Chandragupta Maurya. The work is attributed to Pushyagupta, a provincial governor described in the inscription as a Vaishya. This establishes that the lake was a Mauryan-period public work rather than a new project begun by Rudradaman.

Improvements under Ashoka

During the reign of Ashoka, another governor, Tushaspha, arranged additional water channels or conduits associated with the reservoir. The inscription describes Tushaspha as a Yavana. The name identifies the official mentioned in the record; it does not mean that Ashoka personally supervised the construction.

Damage and repair under Rudradaman

In Shaka year 72, exceptionally heavy rain and flooding damaged the reservoir's embankment. The floodwaters came from streams associated with the Girnar hills. The breach caused the stored water to escape.

Rudradaman ordered the damaged embankment to be rebuilt. The work was carried out under Suvishakha, his appointed governor of Anarta and Saurashtra. The inscription describes Suvishakha as a Pahlava.

According to the royal record, the restoration was financed from the ruler's own resources and was completed without imposing additional taxes or compulsory labour on the population for the repair. This statement describes the funding of the particular project. It must not be interpreted as a claim that Rudradaman abolished taxation generally.

Another repair under Skandagupta

The history of the reservoir continued after the Western Kshatrapas. During the reign of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta, the embankment again suffered damage from flooding in the middle of the 5th century CE.

The later Junagadh inscription records that Parnadatta was the Gupta governor of Saurashtra and that his son Chakrapalita supervised the repair. This restoration is associated with approximately 456–457 CE.

The same rock preserves different historical periods

The inscribed rock near Girnar is associated with records from different ruling powers. Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts belong to the Mauryan period and were largely written in Prakrit using Brahmi script. Rudradaman's Sanskrit record belongs to the Western Kshatrapa period. Skandagupta's Sanskrit inscription belongs to the Gupta period.

These records are distinct inscriptions associated with the same historical site. The existence of Ashoka's edicts at Girnar does not make Rudradaman's inscription a Mauryan record.

What the reservoir teaches about administration

The Sudarshana Lake illustrates the importance of water management in ancient Gujarat. Embankments and channels helped store and distribute water in a region where agriculture depended on seasonal rainfall. Damaged waterworks required labour, materials, supervision and expenditure.

Rudradaman's record also identifies the relationship between a king and a provincial governor. The ruler received credit for the public work, but Suvishakha was the official responsible for carrying it out. The later Gupta inscription similarly distinguishes the emperor from the provincial and local officials involved in the restoration.

Prelims focus

  • Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman: Shaka year 72, approximately 150 CE.
  • Language and script: Sanskrit in Brahmi script.
  • Original Sudarshana Lake construction: Pushyagupta under Chandragupta Maurya.
  • Water channels: Tushaspha under Ashoka.
  • Rudradaman-period repair: Carried out by Suvishakha.
  • Gupta-period repair: Chakrapalita under Skandagupta, approximately 456–457 CE.
  • Trap: Rudradaman repaired the lake; he did not originally construct it.

[NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed p. 38, The Sudarshana Lake in Gujarat; F. Kielhorn, Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman, Epigraphia Indica, vol. 8, 1906, pp. 42–49; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Epigraphy, Junagadh Inscription of Rudradaman, module IC/I Epi/29, sections 2–5; J. F. Fleet, Junagadh Rock Inscription of Skandagupta, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, vol. 3, 1888, no. 14, pp. 58–65; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]
